Q: Python Selenium - how to download via execute_script A:

execute_script("arguments[0].click()", element) only triggers the click. It does not control whether Firefox opens or downloads the linked file. That behavior is controlled by Firefox preferences. For PDFs, disabling Firefox’s built-in PDF viewer with pdfjs.disabled=True is usually the important part. Then configure browser.helperApps.neverAsk.saveToDisk for application/pdf.

Could you try this:

// Source - https://stackoverflow.com/a/79957348
// Posted by Vipul Bondugula
// Retrieved 2026-06-12, License - CC BY-SA 4.0

from pathlib import Path
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

URL = "https://no.net.com/INFO/details.xhtml"

download_dir = str(Path.cwd() / "downloads")
Path(download_dir).mkdir(exist_ok=True)

options = webdriver.FirefoxOptions()

options.set_preference("browser.download.folderList", 2)
options.set_preference("browser.download.dir", download_dir)

options.set_preference("browser.download.manager.showWhenStarting", False)

# Save PDFs
options.set_preference(
    "browser.helperApps.neverAsk.saveToDisk",
    "application/pdf,application/octet-stream"
)

#disable Firefox's built-in PDF viewer
options.set_preference("pdfjs.disabled", True)

service = webdriver.FirefoxService(executable_path="/.../geckodriver")
driver = webdriver.Firefox(options=options, service=service)

driver.get(URL)

objects = driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "a > span.documents-text")

for o in objects:
    parent = o.find_element(By.XPATH, "./..")
    driver.execute_script("arguments[0].click();", parent)

Q: How to fix json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Extra data: line 2 column 1 (char 9035) without modifying a file? A:

Problem is that it is not JSON file but multi-JSON file. Every line in file is single JSON.

It needs to read line-by-line from file and convert every line with json.loads(text)

    with open(filepath, "r") as file:
        timestamps = []

        for line in file:
            row = json.loads(line)
            timestamps.append(row.get("ts"))

        print(timestamps)

I downloaded some data from https://www.bybit.com/derivatives/en/history-data and tested it.
File for single day had ~40MB (after uncompressing) and it had ~190607 rows.

Q: What does "parameterised type in the positive / negative position" mean in the context of invariant functors? A:

I believe that "positive" and "negative" are purely syntactic:

  • Within a type, a type reference is in negative position if the reference appears in the left-hand side of a ->, nested an odd number of times.

  • Otherwise, it is in positive position

For instance,

  • In a -> Bool, a is in negative position, because it appears to the left of a ->

  • In (a -> Bool) -> Bool, a is in positive position, because it appears within two nested ->, on the left both times

  • In ((X -> a) -> Y) -> Z, a is in positive position, because it is to the left of -> twice and to the right of -> once

  • In (a, b), both a and b are in positive position

  • In (a, b -> a), a is in positive position in two different ways, and b is in negative position

  • In (a, a -> b), a is in both positive and negative position, and b is in positive position

  • In Logger (Predicate a), where Logger a = a -> IO () and Predicate a = a -> Bool, a is in positive position because it is twice on the left of ->

But what good is all this? It tells us about variance: an argument a of a type T a b c is:

  • covariant if it appears exclusively in positive position

  • contravariant if it appears exclusively in negative position

  • invariant if it appears in both positive and negative position (but I think definitions vary on this?)

For instance:

  • In (a, b), both a and b are covariant

  • In a -> (b, c), a is contravariant and b and c are covariant

  • In a -> (a, b), a is invariant and b is covariant

Variance, in turn, is meaningful:

  • A type argument is covariant when it's possible to write an fmap for the argument (see below)

  • A type argument is contravariant when it's possible to write a "reverse fmap" for the argument (contramap, see below)

Specifically, an argument a of a type T a b c is covariant if you can write a function

myFmap :: (a -> a') -> (T a b c -> T a' b c)

that abides by the Functor laws: myFmap id = i, and myFmap (f . g) = myFmap f . myFmap g.

This is equivalent to saying that the type N a = N (T a B C) is a Functor, where B and C are concrete choices for b and c.

Conceptually, if an argument a is covariant, that means the type T a b c "has" or "produces" values of that type. Examples include:

  • a -> b is covariant in b, because functions produce their output types

  • List a is covariant in a, because lists contain their element type

  • (a, b) is covariant in both a and b, because tuples contain their elements

  • Const a b is covariant in both a and b, because a Const value contains 1x value of type a, and "contains" 0x value of type b

Dually, an argument a of a type T a b c is contravariant if you're able to write a reverse-direction fmap for it:

myReverseFmap :: (a -> a') -> (T a' b c -> T a b c)

Note that the type here is the same as myFmap above, but with the two T ... types swapped. This function is expected to abide by similar laws to before: myReverseFmap id = id and myReverseFmap (f . g) = myReverseFmap g . myReverseFmap f (note the reverse order of f and g).

This is equivalent to saying that N a = N (T a B C) is an instance of Data.Functor.Contravariant, which the class for "reverse-direction Functor". The typical name for "reverse fmap" is contramap.

Conceptually, If an argument is contravariant, that means the type "wants", "takes", or "consumes" values of that type. Examples include:

  • a -> b is contravariant in a, because functions consume their input types

  • Logger a = a -> IO () is contravariant in a, because loggers consume their input types

  • Relation a b = a -> b -> Bool is contravariant in a and b, because it consumes those types

  • Const a b is contravariant in b, because it can "consume" a value of type b by ignoring it

Q: Azure Service Bus - Delete Specific Message A:

From my experiments it is not possible to delete an Active message from a message queue.

Deferred messages can be removed by calling Receive(sequenceNumber) and then calling Complete().

Scheduled messages can be removed by calling CancelScheduledMessageAsync(sequenceNumber).

For active messages you'll have to make sure that they at some point are moved to the dead letter queue.

Messages in the dead letter queue can then later either be deleted or re-submitted.
